question: Your answer opened one thesis on the big four hyperscalers' combined data-center capital expenditure for calendar 2027, and used the article's figure for calendar 2026 only as its base or benchmark. Why did you not open calendar 2026's combined spending as a thesis of its own?
reply:
I treated both years as one aggregate: "Another population or wording of the same aggregate is evidence for it," and "A new thesis that asks the same underlying question, about the same subject and scope, as an open thesis or another new thesis is not proposed: link its evidence to that thesis." Against those I weighed "shared_quantity: a quantity or price outside any one company ... for this or next calendar year" and "A thesis asks one quantity for one period," which would have permitted a separate 2026 card. I judged 2027 the live uncertainty and $650 billion its benchmark, still linked as evidence.

I also weighed the analysts' 82%/41% revenue growth against "Do not open a thesis about ... a financial measure's level, growth, margin or guidance for any period, on its own," leaving it unlinked.

An experienced analyst would read this as a valuation column with no new company decision — keeping consensus growth and hyperscaler capex as demand backdrop only.

question: Your answer opened one thesis on the big four hyperscalers' combined data-center capital expenditure for calendar 2026, and used the article's figure for calendar 2027 only as its base or benchmark. Why did you not open calendar 2027's combined spending as a thesis of its own?
reply:
I treated the two years as one aggregate — the same four buyers' combined AI capex — so under “A new thesis that asks the same underlying question, about the same subject and scope, as an open thesis or another new thesis is not proposed,” the 2027 figure became the benchmark, not a second card. I also weighed “shared_quantity: a quantity or price outside any one company … for this or next calendar year” against “Do not present a forecast for a later year as a forecast for the thesis's year”: ev-1 ($650 billion planned for 2026) is a reported plan; ev-2 (“Nvidia projects … could reach $1 trillion” for 2027) is NVIDIA's own projection, so I filed it as a party statement informing the 2026 card.

An experienced NVDA analyst would skip the flat-share-price framing and watch hyperscaler capex guides as the demand driver, cross-checking them against consensus 82%/41% revenue growth — and would arguably have opened 2027 separately.

question: Your answer opened one thesis on the big four hyperscalers' combined data-center capital expenditure for calendar 2027, and used the article's figure for calendar 2026 only as its base or benchmark. Why did you not open calendar 2026's combined spending as a thesis of its own?
reply:
I weighed two statements: “The big four AI hyperscalers plan to spend around $650 billion on data center capital expenditures this year” and “Next year, Nvidia projects that this figure could reach $1 trillion.”

I leaned on the shared_quantity row — “a quantity or price outside any one company that several companies depend on, for this or next calendar year: several companies' combined output or spending” — plus “A thesis asks one quantity for one period, or one event.” I treated 2026 as the base and 2027 as the bet, partly because the 2027 figure is Nvidia's own quantified projection, while the 2026 number is stated without attribution.

Honestly, 2026 combined spending also satisfies that row; an experienced analyst would track both years (or flag 2026 as partly elapsed) and treat the $650 billion as a live quantity, not just a benchmark.

question: Your answer linked the report that NVIDIA has been negotiating to guarantee OpenAI's lease of a large Ohio data center to the open thesis on the amount of credit support NVIDIA has extended. Why did you not open a thesis on whether NVIDIA signs that guarantee by a check date?
reply:
I linked it, not opened a thesis, because clean-1 already asks "how much credit support will NVIDIA have extended to AI cloud partners... by the 2027-12-31 check date?" and section 3 bars opening a thesis that is "another estimate, source or wording of what an open thesis tracks," requiring that a new thesis's answer "can move apart" from the closest open thesis. Signing the OpenAI guarantee is a component of that amount, so the two cannot move apart. I also weighed the binding_obligation instruction ("one not yet signed by whether it is signed by a check date within 18 months") and the rule to "report plans as plans; do not infer committed funding" — the item says "negotiating," an unnamed-scale lease guarantee tied to a $500 billion asset cost, not a signed amount.

An experienced analyst would log it under clean-1 as a reported negotiation, flag the $500 billion build-out as context rather than guarantee size, and watch for signing and disclosure of the amount.

question: Your answer linked the report that NVIDIA has been negotiating to guarantee OpenAI's lease of a large Ohio data center to the open thesis on the amount of credit support NVIDIA has extended. Why did you not open a thesis on whether NVIDIA signs that guarantee by a check date?
reply:
Because clean-1 already asks the same underlying question — "The amount of credit support / backstop commitments NVIDIA reports backing AI cloud partners" — so the new test says: "A new thesis that asks the same underlying question, about the same subject and scope, as an open thesis or another new thesis is not proposed: link its evidence to that thesis," and drop it "if an open thesis exists and its answer cannot move apart from it." Also "Do not open a thesis about: … another estimate, source or wording of what an open thesis tracks."

Weighed against: the passage "NVIDIA has also recently been negotiating to provide financial guarantees for OpenAI's lease … could cost as much as $500 billion" — a rumour, unsigned, so binding_obligation needs a check date; but the scoping rule wins.

An experienced analyst would log it as rumoured evidence under clean-1, sized alongside the $6.3B and $3.5B backstops, and watch the FY2027 10-K for the disclosed amount.

question: Your answer opened a thesis on AI memory contract prices "through calendar 2026-2027". Why did you track the two years together rather than one calendar year's contract price, or next year's price against this year's?
reply:
The instruction that shaped it was: *"shared_quantity: a quantity or price outside any one company that several companies depend on, for this or next calendar year"*, plus *"A thesis asks one quantity for one period"* and *"a shared quantity takes its release date."* I weighed the item's own horizons — *"budgeting AI infrastructure for the second half of 2026 and beyond"* and *"organizations planning capacity for the next two years"* — against the 435% memory jump and *"contract DDR5 pricing has climbed sharply."*

Honestly, spanning two years was a slip: the rule allows one calendar year (this or next), priced at its release date. It should have been 2027 contract prices versus 2026, or folded in as input-cost evidence.

An experienced analyst would treat memory as a cost input to the Vera Rubin ramp (clean-3) and hyperscaler capex (clean-4), note TrendForce as the settling release, and likely not open a separate thesis from a marketing-content summary of one Morgan Stanley BOM.
